Scratch test (since deleted): after deletePrescription(), getPrescriptions() returned 0 rows, getDailyDoseSchedule returned 1 slot for the deleted rx, takeDose succeeded, and the deleted inventory item's currentStock went 30 -> 29. LIVE: list_recent_doses has 81 'taken' logs for prescription b194a930 'Sacubitril/valsartan' with archived=true, running through 2026-08-25. On 2026-08-10/13/14/18/25 the same 08:30/20:30 slot was logged 'taken' for both b194a930 (archived) and bddbea47 'Sacubitril/Valsartan' (active, 200 mg), with identical actionTimestamp (e.g. 1787682600000).
---
[analytics-history-export#5] const activePrescriptions = allPrescriptions.filter(p => p.isActive === true);
...where("status").equals("active")
const enabledSchedules = allSchedules.filter(s => s.enabled === true);

Probe P1: after deletePrescription(rx) -> adherenceRate(last 7d) total 8, taken 0; rx.isActive true, deletedAt set.
failure_scenario: The user deletes a medication they stopped taking. It keeps showing as a due dose on today's schedule, web reminders ('Time for X') keep firing, the refill alert can fire ('0 pills left', because its transactions were hard-deleted, see the separate finding), and AI insights keep listing it as an active medication. The same happens for a single dose time the user deleted.
suggested_fix: Make delete also set isActive=false, status='cancelled' and enabled=false, and backfill existing tombstoned rows in a Dexie upgrade. Longer term, give each medication entity one lifecycle field instead of three overlapping booleans/enums plus deletedAt, and route every read through shared 'live' selectors that are tested with deleted fixtures.
verifier_corrections:
The main claim is right, but some of the listed read paths are overstated.

- **`getDailySchedule`** (medication-schedule-service.ts:49) filters schedules on `s.deletedAt === null`. A single deleted dose time therefore does not come back through this function. It only leaks deleted prescriptions and phases.
- **`analytics-snapshot.ts:61`** likewise drops deleted schedules. Deleted prescriptions only reach AI insights through `getActivePrescriptions` and `getActivePhaseForPrescription`. A lone deleted dose time does not show up there.
- **Deleted single dose times** do still leak through `getDailyDoseSchedule` and `checkDoseReminders`, as the finding says.
- **`use-timezone-detection`** was named as a read path, but I did not verify it.

Some of the listed read paths are overstated. medication-schedule-service.ts:49 getDailySchedule does filter `s.deletedAt === null`, so deleted schedules drop out there. It still keeps deleted prescriptions and phases, because it filters on isActive and status only. Likewise, analytics-snapshot.ts:61 filters schedules by deletedAt, but the deleted prescription and phase still get into AI insights through getActivePrescriptions and getActivePhaseForPrescription. So the deleted-schedule part applies to getDailyDoseSchedule and checkDoseReminders, but not to getDailySchedule or the snapshot. I did not reproduce the refill-alert '0 pills left' claim here; it depends on the separate finding about hard-deleted transactions.

The "deleted schedules" half is overstated. deleteSchedule (medication-schedule-service.ts:154) is only reachable through useDeleteSchedule, and no component uses that hook; only a test calls it. So the user can't delete a single dose time from the UI, and the claim that "the same happens for a single dose time the user deleted" can't happen through the app. Two further corrections:
- medication-schedule-service.ts:49 (getDailySchedule) does filter deletedAt. It should not be listed as a path that ignores it.
- analytics-snapshot.ts:61 filters deletedAt on schedules. AI insights leak only through getActivePrescriptions and getActivePhaseForPrescription.

The refill-alert claim depends on a separate finding and I did not verify it here.

title: The app-launch stock recount adds soft-deleted inventory transactions back in, so deleted refills return
description: getCurrentStock sums every transaction for an item, including soft-deleted ones. deleteInventoryTransaction and updateInventoryTransaction correctly filter `deletedAt === null`, but recalculateAllStock runs on every app launch (initStockRecalculation in Providers) and overwrites the stored stock total (`currentStock`) with the unfiltered sum. The earlier Fable plan called this omission a 'latent bug'. It is still present at HEAD and the UI can trigger it: the inventory drawer has a delete button for each transaction.
evidence:
inventory-service.ts:269 `const transactions = await db.inventoryTransactions.where("inventoryItemId").equals(inventoryItemId).toArray(); const sum = transactions.reduce((acc, tx) => acc + tx.amount, 0);`. Scratch test: initial 30 + refill 100, deleteInventoryTransaction(refill) gave currentStock=30, then recalculateAllStock() gave currentStock=130.
---
[prescriptions-model#2] inventory-service.ts:274 `const sum = transactions.reduce((acc, tx) => acc + tx.amount, 0);` (no deletedAt filter) vs :235 `.filter(t => t.deletedAt === null && t.id !== id)`. providers.tsx:58 `initStockRecalculation();`. Scratch test: refill +60 then delete it -> `STOCK AFTER DELETE 30`; after recalculateAllStock -> `STOCK AFTER LAUNCH RECALC 90`.
---
[doses-titration-schedule#15] `const sum = transactions.reduce((acc, tx) => acc + tx.amount, 0);` with no deletedAt filter. Probe: stock 30, add +10 refill, delete it → 30; recalculateAllStock → 40.
failure_scenario: The user logs a refill of 100 pills by mistake and deletes it (stock shows 30). On the next app launch stock jumps back to 130, refill alerts stay quiet, and days-of-supply is overstated by 100 pills. The recount also stamps a new updatedAt and pushes the wrong value to the server.
suggested_fix: Filter `t.deletedAt === null` in getCurrentStock. Better still, stop storing `currentStock` and derive stock from transactions in one shared helper that both the client and the MCP SQL use.
verifier_corrections: I lowered severity from critical to high. `currentStock` is a cached value that can be rebuilt from the transactions, so no source data is lost. The server-side MCP `getInventoryStatus` already derives stock correctly from non-deleted transactions. The harm is wrong stock counts, days-of-supply and refill alerts in the client UI, and a wrong `currentStock` synced to the server. That is wrong data on screen, not dosing information. The file list in the finding also repeats overlapping line ranges. The key lines are inventory-service.ts:268-276 (the bug), :233-235 (the correct filter used on delete), :299-345 and :351 (the recount on launch), and providers.tsx:53-58.

The files list has duplicate and overlapping line ranges. The core claims are accurate. One overstatement: this is not unrecoverable data loss, because the soft-deleted rows remain and a correct filtered recount restores the right value. I lowered the severity from critical to high for that reason. The wrong `currentStock` is still persisted and pushed to the server on every launch after a transaction is deleted.

Severity is overstated: this is not data loss or wrong dosing information. It shows the wrong stock count and silences refill alerts, and it can be recovered because the soft-deleted rows are kept, so high rather than critical. It only happens after a manual transaction delete in the inventory drawer; dose undo is not affected because it uses compensating transactions. The files list contains duplicate and overlapping line ranges. The main locations are inventory-service.ts:268-276 (getCurrentStock), :299-345 (recalculateAllStock) and providers.tsx:52-59.

title: Hard deletes of dose logs, inventory transactions and edited-out schedules never reach the server
description: deletePrescription hard-deletes every doseLog and inventoryTransaction for the prescription (`.delete()`) and enqueues nothing for them. updatePhase hard-deletes (bulkDelete) the schedules removed from the form and enqueues 'delete'. With the local row gone, the sync engine sends a stub `{id, deletedAt, updatedAt}`, which the server validates against the full insert schema and rejects as invalid, so the op is dropped. Any queued upserts for hard-deleted rows are skipped by `if (!liveRow) continue;` and never acked. The cleanup of those orphaned queue rows was also being probed by the sync auditor, so it is not repeated here.
evidence:
prescription-service.ts:146 `await db.doseLogs.where("prescriptionId").equals(id).delete();`, 150 `await db.inventoryTransactions.where("inventoryItemId").equals(item.id).delete();`. phase-service.ts:269 `await db.phaseSchedules.bulkDelete(toDelete);`. Scratch zod parse of the stub `{tableName:'phaseSchedules', op:'delete', row:{id,deletedAt,updatedAt}}` against opSchema_ gave success:false, missing phaseId, time, scheduleTimeUTC, anchorTimezone, dosage, daysOfWeek, enabled, createdAt, deviceId.
---
[sync-engine#5] phase-service.ts:270 `await db.phaseSchedules.bulkDelete(toDelete); for (const sid of toDelete) await enqueueInsideTx("phaseSchedules", sid, "delete");`. sync-engine.ts:177 `const row = liveRow ?? { id: qRow.recordId, deletedAt: qRow.enqueuedAt, updatedAt: qRow.enqueuedAt };`. Scratch test: `opSchema_.safeParse({queueId:1, tableName:'phaseSchedules', op:'delete', row:{id:'x',deletedAt:1,updatedAt:1}}).success === false`.
failure_scenario: (1) The user removes the 20:00 dose from a phase in Edit medication. It disappears locally, but the server keeps the schedule live, so MCP list_medications and any freshly synced device still show and schedule the 20:00 dose. (2) Deleting a prescription permanently destroys its whole adherence history on the device, while the server keeps those dose logs and transactions live. They show in MCP list_recent_doses, and in the inventory SUM for the (soft-deleted) item.
suggested_fix: Never hard-delete synced tables. Soft-delete children with deletedAt and updatedAt and enqueue them. If a hard delete is ever needed, make the delete-op schema a separate `{id, deletedAt, updatedAt}` shape that the server accepts.
verifier_corrections: Minor precision fixes only. The 'delete' op on a hard-deleted schedule is not just dropped silently. It is rejected with code "invalid", and the client then removes it from the queue permanently. For deletePrescription, dose logs and inventory transactions are never enqueued at all, so no stub is ever sent for them. The server row simply stays live. The finding cites the same ranges more than once (phase-service 268-273/269-273, sync-engine 174-192/174-181, prescription-service 146-151/146-150), but they point to the same code.

The file list repeats the same locations with slightly different line ranges. The substance is accurate.

One detail in failure scenario (2) is unverified. Whether MCP list_recent_doses actually shows the orphaned dose logs depends on whether that query also filters by the parent prescription's deletedAt, which I did not check. The server rows being live is confirmed either way.

A note on wording: the local adherence history is destroyed on the device only. It survives on the server. The finding says this, but the net effect is divergence between device and server, not total loss of the data.

Nothing material. One small addition: the finding lists the inventory SUM for the soft-deleted item as a symptom, but that item is itself tombstoned on the server, so it only matters if something sums transactions without filtering on the parent. The resurrected schedule on reinstall or a fresh-device pull is the more serious user-facing effect, and the finding should call it out explicitly.

title: Stock is stored twice (`currentStock` and the transaction history) and every launch pushes the stored total over newer data from other devices
description: The type says `@deprecated Use inventoryTransactions sum`, yet every UI and alert reads `currentStock`, and doses do a read-modify-write on it (`(inventory.currentStock ?? 0) - pillsConsumed`). `currentStock` syncs as its own last-write-wins field, and recalculateAllStock stamps `updatedAt: Date.now()` on every item at every launch, possibly before the first pull has finished. The client total and the server/MCP total also diverge: the server uses the sum of non-deleted transactions cast `::int`, while the client uses the unfiltered sum.
evidence:
records.ts: `/** @deprecated Use inventoryTransactions sum. Will be removed in Phase 3. */ currentStock?: number;`. inventory-service.ts:313 `await db.inventoryItems.update(item.id, { currentStock: newStock, updatedAt: Date.now() }); await enqueueInsideTx("inventoryItems", item.id, "upsert");` (all items, every launch). mcp/queries.ts `SELECT SUM(amount)::int ... AND deletedAt IS NULL`.
---
[prescriptions-model#15] inventory-service.ts:313-317 `await db.inventoryItems.update(item.id, { currentStock: newStock, updatedAt: Date.now() }); await enqueueInsideTx("inventoryItems", item.id, "upsert");` runs for every item, every launch.
failure_scenario: Device B logs doses offline. Device A opens the app, recounts with its stale transaction set and pushes currentStock with a newer updatedAt. B's pull then overwrites B's correct total with A's stale one, so pill counts and refill alerts are wrong until some later relaunch. MCP get_inventory_status reports 29 when the app shows 29.5 (half-pill doses are truncated by ::int).
suggested_fix: Remove `currentStock` from the synced schema. Derive stock from non-deleted transactions everywhere (one helper, with a LiveQuery sum), or keep it as a device-local, unsynced cache. Use `numeric`/real without the ::int cast on the server.
verifier_corrections: Two small corrections. First, `::int` in PostgreSQL rounds rather than truncates: 29.5 becomes 30, not 29. The mismatch between MCP and the app is still real. Second, the finding leaves out the clearest failure, which needs only one device. `getCurrentStock` includes soft-deleted transactions, so after a user deletes a transaction in the inventory drawer, the next app launch's `recalculateAllStock` adds it back and the stock silently reverts. That failure is concrete, easy to reproduce, and more certain than the cross-device race. The race itself is valid, but the wrong value only lasts until a later relaunch recalculates.

- **The rounding example is wrong.** The column is `real`, and Postgres rounds a float to the nearest whole number when casting to int (ties go to the even number); it does not truncate. So 29.5 shows as 30, not 29, and 28.5 shows as 28. The conclusion still holds: the MCP total is lossy and doesn't match the app.
- **The finding understates the unfiltered sum.** It's not only a client/server mismatch. On the client itself, it brings back soft-deleted transactions after a relaunch, and that corrupted value is then pushed to other devices; the scratch test proves this. That is the strongest concrete failure here.
- **The "until some later relaunch" claim needs a caveat.** A relaunch only fixes the total if that device's own transaction set is complete and has no deleted rows.

1) The `::int` cast on the server's SUM (mcp/queries.ts:561) rounds rather than truncates. Postgres float-to-int uses round-half-to-even, so 29.5 becomes 30 (and 28.5 becomes 28), not 29 as the finding says. The mismatch is still real: `amount` is `real` (schema.ts:561), so half-pill balances are misreported by up to 0.5.
2) The multi-device overwrite is temporary rather than persistent. Another relaunch after the pull recomputes stock from the now-complete transaction set, so it is only "wrong until a later relaunch".
3) The finding undersells the deleted-transaction case, which is the most concrete impact. Because `getCurrentStock` does not filter `deletedAt`, each cold start adds soft-deleted transaction amounts back into `currentStock` and syncs the result. This happens on a single device with no concurrency, through the UI path in inventory-item-view-drawer.tsx.

title: The v12 migration's keyword matching invents caffeine/alcohol records, which are never linked to their water record
description: v12 turned intake notes into SubstanceRecords with raw substring matching (`note.includes(kw)`). Keywords such as 'tea', 'gin', 'rum', 'wine' and 'spirit' also match 'steak', 'instead', 'ginger', 'original', 'drum', 'spirulina'. 'Long Island iced tea' is classified as caffeine because caffeine is checked first. The created substances are linked only by `sourceRecordId`, which nothing reads except MCP. The v22 repair only covers `source startsWith 'substance:'` pairs, so v12 pairs never get a groupId.
evidence:
`const caffeineMatch = CAFFEINE_KEYWORDS.find((kw) => note.includes(kw));` with CAFFEINE_KEYWORDS containing 'tea' and ALCOHOL_KEYWORDS containing 'gin', 'rum'. grep: `sourceRecordId` is used only in db.ts and mcp/queries.ts:399.
---
[substance-sugar#11] `const caffeineMatch = CAFFEINE_KEYWORDS.find((kw) => note.includes(kw));` with `CAFFEINE_KEYWORDS = ['coffee','espresso','tea',...]`, `ALCOHOL_KEYWORDS = [... 'gin', 'rum', ...]`; v22 only scans `.where("source").startsWith("substance:")`.
failure_scenario: A pre-v12 water entry with note 'ginger water' became a 1-standard-drink alcohol record; 'water instead of coffee' became 95 mg caffeine. Deleting or editing the original water entry leaves the phantom substance counting toward daily caffeine/alcohol totals and AI insights.
suggested_fix: Add a one-off repair: list v12-created substances (deviceId 'migrated-v12' or source 'water_intake' with sourceRecordId), let the user review or bulk-delete them, and backfill groupId from sourceRecordId so cascades work.
verifier_corrections: One example is wrong: 'spirulina' does NOT contain 'spirit' (s-p-i-r-u vs s-p-i-r-i), so it is not a false match. The rest hold: 'steak'/'instead' match 'tea', 'ginger'/'original' match 'gin', 'drum' matches 'rum', and 'Long Island iced tea' becomes caffeine. Two points to add. First, the AI enrichment pass (substance-enrich.ts) is dead code with no callers, so these rows keep their default keyword amounts forever. Second, `sourceRecordId` is also a server-side FK in packages/db/src/schema.ts:245, not just an MCP field. Neither point changes the verdict.

'spirulina' does not contain 'spirit' (s-p-i-r-u vs s-p-i-r-i), so that example is wrong; the other examples hold. 'water instead of coffee' is right about the 95 mg, but it matches on 'coffee', not on the 'tea' inside 'instead'. The finding misses that the AI enrichment pass (`runSubstanceEnrichment`) meant to follow v12 is never called anywhere, so these records also keep their default amounts. The finding also lists overlapping line ranges twice; the relevant spots are db.ts:283-351 (v12) and db.ts ~555-650 (v22).

title: Indexes on boolean fields (isActive, enabled) never match, and the debug stock panel queries one
description: `prescriptions.isActive`, `inventoryItems.isActive` and `phaseSchedules.enabled` are indexed, but the values are JS booleans, which are not valid IndexedDB keys, so those index entries are never created. Services know this and load whole tables instead (see the comment at dose-log-service.ts:282). The debug panel still queries the index.
evidence: db.ts `prescriptions: "id, isActive, updatedAt, createdAt"`, `phaseSchedules: "id, phaseId, time, enabled, updatedAt"`. debug-panel.tsx:289 `db.inventoryItems.where("isActive").equals(1).toArray()`.
failure_scenario: The Debug > Stock Management comparison list is always empty, so the drift check can't show drift. Every medication read is a full table scan.
suggested_fix: Store these flags as 0/1 numbers (or replace them with a lifecycle enum string, which is indexable), and drop the dead indexes in a new version.
verifier_corrections: This is minor. The "every medication read is a full table scan" point is a perf remark, not a user-visible failure. The tables are small single-user data, and the services scan in memory on purpose. The only functional breakage is the debug panel's Compare Cached vs Derived list, which is always empty. The Recalculate All Stock drift report still works.

title: deletedAt: null cannot be indexed, so every active-record read loads the whole table
description: deletedAt uses null for 'live', and null is not an IndexedDB key, so no compound like [deletedAt+timestamp] is possible. Every list and paginated read (getAllRecords, getRecordsPaginated, getRecordsByCursor, getWeightRecords, getLatestWeightRecord, getActiveRecords) does `orderBy('timestamp').toArray()` and then filters in memory. That is the root cause of the forgotten-filter bugs above: nothing forces callers to exclude tombstones.
evidence: intake-service.ts:137 `// Load all non-deleted records, then apply offset/limit manually... Data volume is small`. getLatestWeightRecord: `db.weightRecords.orderBy("timestamp").reverse().toArray(); return records.find(...)`.
failure_scenario: A multi-year user with tens of thousands of intake rows reloads the whole table for every dashboard or history query, and every Dexie liveQuery re-runs on each write. Separately, any new query that forgets the JS filter shows deleted data (already happening in the medication domain).
suggested_fix: Add an indexable live flag (e.g. `isDeleted: 0|1`, or `deletedAt: 0` for live) and compound indexes such as [isDeleted+timestamp] and [isDeleted+type+timestamp]. Wrap reads in a per-table `live()` collection helper.
verifier_corrections:
- "Every active-record read loads the whole table" is false. Date-range reads (getRecordsByDateRange, getWeightRecordsByDateRange, getRecordsBetween) use the timestamp index. Only the newest-N list reads scan the whole table.
- getAllRecords, getRecordsPaginated and getLatestWeightRecord have no production UI callers. The reachable full scans are getRecordsByCursor/useHistoryData, getWeightRecords (useLatestWeight, useWeightRecords) and getActiveRecords (eating, urination, defecation).
- The impact is performance/latency only, with no incorrect data, so medium is too high; low is appropriate.
- The "root cause of forgotten-filter bugs" claim is opinion: an index would not force callers to filter.
- The suggested fix is heavier than needed. Dexie's `Collection.filter().limit(n)` stops scanning early without a schema migration. Only offset-based pagination needs a different approach, such as a cursor.

1. Loading the whole table is not forced by null being unindexable. Dexie's `filter()` + `limit()` streams over the timestamp index and stops early, so the cursor and limit functions could avoid full loads without a schema change.
2. `getRecordsPaginated`, `getLatestWeightRecord` and `getAllRecords` have no production callers. The only reachable full scans are `getRecordsByCursor`, `getWeightRecords` and `getActiveRecords`.
3. The date-range queries (`getRecordsBetween`, `getWeightRecordsByDateRange`) already use the timestamp index.
4. No concrete user-visible failure is shown for realistic single-user data volumes. Severity should be low, and the "root cause of the forgotten-filter bugs" claim is a design opinion, not evidence.

title: Audit log grows without limit and syncs to the server; every launch adds a row and pushes every inventory item
description: auditLogs has no retention. Every medication mutation, AI parse and settings change appends a synced row, and recalculateAllStock writes a `stock_recalculated` entry on every app launch, plus one push per inventory item even when nothing drifted. _errorLogs has an LRU cap; auditLogs has none. It is also in backup/restore.
evidence: inventory-service.ts:333 `await writeAuditLog("stock_recalculated", {...})` called from initStockRecalculation() in providers.tsx on every mount. No `auditLogs` delete/prune exists apart from the debug panel's local `db.auditLogs.clear()`, which does not sync.
failure_scenario: After a year of daily use there are thousands of audit rows plus 365+ stock_recalculated rows. They inflate backups, sync pulls on new devices and Neon storage, and the updatedAt churn on inventoryItems causes the cross-device overwrites described in the stock finding.
suggested_fix: Write stock_recalculated only when something drifted, and skip the item update when stock is unchanged. Add a retention window (e.g. 180 days) or make auditLogs device-local and unsynced.
verifier_corrections:
1. Not every audit write is synced. The medication, inventory, dose and titration services use buildAuditEntry or writeAuditLog, and those rows are queued for sync. But logAudit() in lib/audit.ts, used for AI parse (ai-client.ts), manual input, weight/BP cards, backup and the add-medication form, does a plain `db.auditLogs.bulkAdd(entries)` with no enqueue. Those rows stay on the device and only reach the server if a later full push picks them up. Unsynced local rows still grow without limit.
2. Saying no prune exists at all is slightly off. A retention function, `purgeOldAuditLogs` (audit.ts:103, 90-day default), does exist and is tested, but nothing ever calls it. It is dead code, and the fix is to call it (and have it propagate deletes to sync) rather than write a new one.
3. The "365+ stock_recalculated rows per year" figure is a lower bound. It fires on every Providers mount (every cold start or full reload), not once a day.

(1) New devices do not pull audit logs. The sync pull route explicitly excludes them (apps/web/src/app/api/sync/pull/route.ts:71: `.filter(t => t !== 'auditLogs')`), so the claim that sync pulls on new devices get inflated is wrong. The extra rows only affect push traffic, Neon storage and backups. (2) Not every audit write is synced. logAudit() in apps/web/src/lib/audit.ts writes straight to `db.auditLogs.bulkAdd` with no sync-queue step. That path covers AI parse (ai-client.ts), weight and blood-pressure cards, manual input, backup and the add-medication form, and those rows stay on the device. Only the writeAuditLog/buildAuditEntry paths push to the server: medication, inventory, dose, phase, titration and the stock_recalculated entry. (3) The finding says no prune exists. A retention function, purgeOldAuditLogs, does exist in audit.ts:101, but nothing calls it, so it is dead code. (4) The strongest part of the finding is not the audit rows. It is that every inventory item gets a fresh updatedAt and a push on each launch even when nothing drifted, which feeds last-write-wins overwrites across devices.

title: The deprecated PhaseSchedule.time is still indexed and used as the source of truth in several places
description: Each schedule stores the same time twice, as `time` (local HH:MM, marked deprecated) and `scheduleTimeUTC`. The web notifier and getDailySchedule group by `time`. The daily dose list and Android use `scheduleTimeUTC`. Dose logs key on `scheduledTime` (a string). No invariant keeps them consistent, and the two drift apart after any DST change (see the DST finding). `time` keeps its index while scheduleTimeUTC has none.
evidence: records.ts `/** @deprecated Use scheduleTimeUTC. Kept for v10 DB record compatibility. */ time: string;`. medication-notification-service.ts `const timeParts = schedule.time.split(":")`. dose-schedule-service.ts:188 `formatLocalTime(schedule.scheduleTimeUTC, tz)`.
failure_scenario: In summer the web reminder fires at 08:00 (from `time`), the medication list shows the slot at 09:00 (from UTC minutes), and a dose logged from the list gets scheduledTime '09:00'. Adherence history then shows two different times for the same dose.
suggested_fix: Keep one canonical local time field. Derive every other representation from it.
verifier_corrections: getDailySchedule is dead code (called only in medication-schedule-service.test.ts), so it isn't a live source of truth. In practice only the web reminder (medication-notification-service.ts) reads `time`. The cited dose-log-service.ts:109-127 does not read PhaseSchedule.time. It matches on the scheduledTime string that callers pass in (slot.localTime, which is derived from scheduleTimeUTC). Dose logs join to slots by prescription/phase/schedule ID, not by time, so drift does not orphan logs. The damage is limited to reminder times that don't match the list and scheduledTime strings that change across a DST boundary. It largely overlaps with the separate DST finding.

1. `getDailySchedule` (medication-schedule-service.ts:29), which groups by `time`, is dead in production. Its only callers are tests, so the list of affected places should drop it. The live consumer of `time` is the web notifier, which does run.
2. The daily dose list matches logs using the key prescription|phase|schedule, which has no time in it (dose-schedule-service.ts:183). So a status in the list still finds its log even when the two times disagree. The visible harm is:
   - the reminder fires an hour away from the time the list shows;
   - `scheduledTime` values in logs, and the `getDoseLogRaw` lookup that filters by time, depend on which path created the log.
3. The root cause is shared with the DST finding: `getTimezoneOffsetMinutes` uses the current offset. This finding is best read as the "two sources of truth" consequence of that bug, not an independent one.

title: The IntakeRecord 'salt' type stores sodium mg, and units are implicit and differ per type
description: `type: 'salt'` actually holds sodium mg (inputs are named saltMg and SODIUM_SOURCE, and the prompt says 'in mg sodium NOT salt'), while the type comment says 'mg for salt'. The unit of `amount` depends on type (ml, mg, g) and is never stored. The server column is `integer`, but the TS type is `number` and only some write paths round: drink-service rounds, addIntakeRecord does not.
evidence: records.ts `amount: number; // ml for water, mg for salt, g for sugar, mg for potassium`. drink-service.ts `{ type: "salt", raw: input.saltMg, source: SODIUM_SOURCE }`. schema.ts `amount: integer("amount").notNull()`. intake-service.ts addIntakeRecord stores `amount` unrounded.
failure_scenario: Any consumer that reads 'salt' literally, such as a future export, AI prompt or chart label, is off by a factor of about 2.5 (1 g salt ≈ 400 mg sodium). A fractional sugar or potassium amount entered through addIntakeRecord is rejected by the server's integer column and silently dropped from sync.
suggested_fix: Rename the enum to 'sodium' in a migration, or add an explicit `unit` column. Enforce integer amounts in one write helper.
verifier_corrections: The finding's example is the wrong one. It names a fractional sugar or potassium amount entered through addIntakeRecord. The concrete reachable path is voice-panel.tsx:196-209: voice-logged water (oz→ml conversion, e.g. 8 oz → 236.588 ml) and voice-logged salt (`item.sodiumMg`) are passed unrounded to addIntakeRecord. The sync push rejects them with `code: "invalid"`, and sync-engine.ts:331 drops them permanently. The record stays only in local IndexedDB. The voice panel's food branch does round (lines 281-301). The 'salt' naming issue is misleading documentation plus a latent risk to future consumers, not a present bug.

The failure scenario names the wrong input path. Fractional sugar or potassium does not reach `addIntakeRecord`: voice rounds them, and the other writers go through the composable or drink services. The unrounded path is voice "water" (`item.ml`, e.g. an oz→ml conversion giving 236.588) and voice "salt" (`item.sodiumMg`) in `voice-panel.tsx:196-209`. Those amounts pass `addIntakeRecord` unrounded, fail the server's `z.int()` push validation, and are dropped from sync as "invalid". The naming problem is also not only a future risk: the MCP `get_today_summary` returns sodium as `salt_mg` (`apps/web/src/lib/mcp/queries.ts:143`) to an AI consumer right now.

title: Enum-like fields and foreign keys are stored as free strings
description: Several fields are typed as bare strings in both the types and the server: amountEstimate (the UI only writes small/medium/large), groupSource (the comment lists 3 values), unit, and IntakeRecord.source, which packs foreign keys and categories into one string ('substance:<id>', 'preset:<id>', 'food:apple', 'manual:sodium'). DoseLog.scheduledDate and scheduledTime are local date/time strings, while every other table uses Unix ms plus timezone.
evidence: `source?: string; // "manual", "food:apple", "voice", etc.`, `amountEstimate?: string;`, `groupSource?: string; // "ai_food_parse" | "ai_substance_lookup" | "manual"`. v22 needed `.where("source").startsWith("substance:")` to recover a relationship.
failure_scenario: Relationship repairs such as v22 have to parse strings. A typo or new value such as 'Medium' passes type-checking and sync, and then breaks grouping or filters. Cascades by id can't be indexed properly.
suggested_fix: Promote these to literal-union types with CHECK constraints on the server. Replace the `source` prefixes with explicit columns (sourceKind, presetId, linkedRecordId). Store dose-log scheduled instants as ms plus timezone.
verifier_corrections: The failure scenario is speculative. No current writer produces off-list values such as "Medium", and nothing groups or filters on amountEstimate or groupSource in a way that would break. "Cascades by id can't be indexed properly" is false for `source`: it is indexed, and the v22 lookup uses an index-backed `startsWith` range query. Treating the local-string `scheduledDate`/`scheduledTime` as an inconsistency ignores that they are intentional wall-clock slot keys, with `actionTimestamp` holding the actual instant. The claim that CHECK constraints are missing applies only to amount_estimate and group_source. The server already constrains most other enum columns. This should be classed as a latent design-hygiene issue with low severity, not as an observed defect.

title: The `timezone` backfilled by v11 and added by syncFields exists on tables whose types and server schema have no such field
description: v11 wrote `timezone` onto prescriptions, medicationPhases and phaseSchedules, and syncFields() adds timezone to every new record. The Prescription, MedicationPhase, PhaseSchedule, TitrationPlan, UserProfile and InsightReport types omit it, and so do their server tables. The data lives only on the device and is dropped by drizzle-zod on push. Timezone presence is inconsistent across the 16 tables: some have `timezone`, schedules have `anchorTimezone`, some have nothing.
evidence: db.ts:256 `await backfillTimezone("prescriptions", "createdAt");`. schema.ts:309 `// NOTE: no timezone column — Prescription interface ... omits it.`
failure_scenario: Features such as 'when/where was this phase started' can't rely on the field, because it is present on old local rows and missing after any sync round-trip or restore on a new device.
suggested_fix: Decide on a per-table timezone policy, then add the field to the types and server or strip it locally in a migration.
verifier_corrections: The finding's failure scenario is hypothetical. No code reads `timezone` on prescriptions, phases, schedules or titration plans, so no user sees a wrong result. The server-side omission is intentional and documented in schema.ts comments (lines 309, 337, 378, 426, 657, 690), so it is not an oversight. The field is not stored on UserProfile or InsightReport rows, and I found no evidence that it is. Those types are only listed as omitting it. The real issue is small: v11 and syncFields() write an extra untyped field on some tables that is dropped on sync. It is latent inconsistency only, and the fix is cosmetic (stop spreading `timezone` into these tables, or strip it).

title: Sync push upsert lets one account take over another account's row with the same id (ownership and LWW bypass)
description: Every synced table's primary key is `id` alone (not (user_id, id)). The push route looks up existing rows with `WHERE id IN (...) AND user_id = me`, so it never sees a row with that id owned by someone else. It then runs `insert ... onConflictDoUpdate({ target: id, set: { ...row, userId: me } })`. The conflict branch fires on the other user's row and rewrites every column, including user_id. The LWW comparison is skipped completely because serverRow is undefined. Sign-out does not clear Dexie, `_syncQueue` or `_syncMeta`, and the migration wizard pushes every local row. So the same device used by two whitelisted accounts, or one backup imported into two accounts, moves records between accounts. Inner FKs also accept cross-user references: a dose log owned by A can point at B's prescription.
evidence:
push/route.ts: `.where(and(inArray(table.id, chunk), eq(table.userId, auth.userId!)))` ... `writeValues = {...rowWithoutUserId, userId: auth.userId!, updatedAt}` ... `.onConflictDoUpdate({ target: table.id, set: setValues })`.
Real-Postgres probe: user-A pushed intake id 'shared-id' (amount 250, updatedAt T). user-B pushed the same id (amount 1, updatedAt T-5), which was ACCEPTED. Result: `select user_id, amount from intake_records where id='shared-id'` → `[{user_id:'user-B', amount:1}]`. Cross-FK probe: user-A's doseLog with prescriptionId of user-B's rx was also accepted.
failure_scenario: Owner signs out on a shared tablet, and a second whitelisted user signs in and runs the migration wizard (or has queued ops left over). Every id that already exists server-side for the owner is reassigned to the second user and overwritten. The rows disappear from the owner's pulls and MCP queries, and the second account now holds the owner's medical data.
suggested_fix: Add a guard to the conflict update: `.onConflictDoUpdate({ target: id, set, where: eq(table.userId, auth.userId) })`. Treat a 0-row result as a rejected op with code 'conflict'. Better: make the PK composite (user_id, id), or at minimum add UNIQUE (user_id, id) and enforce that the conflict owner matches. Also clear `_syncQueue`/`_syncMeta` (and warn about local data) when a different userId signs in.
verifier_corrections: The code mechanism is accurate, but critical overstates the severity. Ids are random UUIDs and pull responses are filtered by user, so no account can target another account's ids. It only happens when two whitelisted accounts push the same local dataset (shared device, or the same backup imported into both). The whitelist is optional: an empty ALLOWED_EMAILS lets any signed-in account through (auth-middleware test case 4), but that alone still does not expose ids. The takeover is silent data loss when triggered, but for a single-user app it is better rated medium than critical. The cited line numbers are approximate but point to the right code.

The bug is real, but the severity is overstated. It needs two whitelisted accounts on one device, or the same backup imported into two accounts, and the app is effectively single-user. The 'real-Postgres probe' in the finding was not re-run here; this verification relies on the code at HEAD plus standard ON CONFLICT semantics. The cross-user FK claim (a dose log pointing at another user's prescription) is plausible from the schema, but it is a separate and lesser issue. The file:line anchors are approximate: the upsert is at about lines 248-256.

The mechanism is accurate, including the missing ownership guard on onConflictDoUpdate and the fact that sign-out does not clear local sync state. The severity is wrong. ALLOWED_EMAILS contains only the owner's email, so it takes two distinct whitelisted accounts to trigger this, and that setup does not exist. It is a latent risk that depends on how the app is deployed, not a critical security or data-loss bug for the current single-user app. The cross-user FK point (a dose log referencing another user's prescription) needs a second account in the same way.

title: Integer columns reject fractional values that client paths write, so those records are silently never synced
description:
intake_records.amount, eating_records.grams, substance_records.amount_mg and volume_ml, and blood_pressure heart_rate are `integer`. drizzle-zod turns these into `z.number().int()`, so any fractional value fails per-op validation. The server returns code 'invalid' and the client drops the op immediately (no retries); the local Dexie row keeps the fraction. Several client paths write non-integers without rounding:
- The voice 'food' path passes the AI's `sugarG`, `sodiumMg`, `potassiumMg`, `waterMl` and `grams` straight through (`z.number()`, not int). The voice caffeine no-volume path is inconsistent: it rounds the solutes but not `caffeineMg`.
- AI enrichment writes `amountMg: data.caffeineMg, volumeMl: data.volumeMl`, validated only as `z.number()`.
- The Records-tab caffeine edit writes `amountMg: parseFloat(...)`.
Other paths (food-section, logDrink, syncEatingGroup) do round, so the same food logged by voice or by form syncs differently. Migration 0020 already fixed the same class of bug for inventory stock; these columns were missed.
evidence:
drizzle-zod probe (opSchema_): intake amount 12.5 → `row.amount: expected int, received number`; substance amountMg 47.5 → rejected; eating grams 150.5 → rejected; heartRate 70.5 → rejected.
voice-panel.tsx: `intakes.push({ type: "sugar", amount: item.sugarG, ...})` (not rounded) versus the no-volume caffeine path `amount: Math.round(item.sugarG)`.
records-tab.tsx:375: `amountField = { amountMg: amt };` where `const amt = parseFloat(editSubstanceAmount)`.
sync-engine: `if (r.code === "invalid" ...) dropIds.push(q.id)`.
---
[liquids-save#8] drink-service.ts: "Postgres stores intake amounts as `integer`; a fractional value is rejected by the push validator and silently dropped by the sync engine". Scratch: addIntakeRecord('water', 333.33) then opSchema_.safeParse ⇒ `false [["row","amount"],"Invalid input: expected int, received number"]`.
---

title: The first 'take' of a scheduled dose writes a consumed inventory transaction with no dose_log_id

title: Edit made while a push is in flight is acked out of the queue and never pushed

title: Pull overwrites pending, newer local edits and the push then sends the stale server copy

The push macrotask will usually read the local rows and send them before the pull's bulkPut lands. In that case the server keeps A's newer edit, but the pull still writes B's older content over A's local copy. applyServerAck (lines 223-226) then updates only updatedAt, so the local row briefly has B's content with A's timestamp until a later pull fixes it. That later pull can be dropped if pullInFlight is still set. So the claim that the push sends the stale copy is reliable for the startup path and the 30-second skew re-scan path, and only possible under some timings for the online event. The 'online' event path is described wrongly. It is true that `schedulePull` (a microtask) starts before `schedulePush(0)` (a setTimeout). But the push reads its live rows from local Dexie right away, while the pull is still waiting for its network response. So in the usual case the push sends the correct local edit and the server keeps it. The pull then briefly overwrites the local row with the older server version. `applyServerAck` only raises `updatedAt` (local 3000 <= server 5000), so for a moment the local row has old content with the new timestamp. The next pull fetches the 5000 row again and corrects it. That path causes temporary wrong data on screen, not permanent loss. The permanent-loss paths are (a) the startup pull, because no push runs at startup, and (b) the one-device case described in the reasoning: the 30 s skew-window re-scan fetches the device's own rows again and overwrites an edit made while a push was in flight. The suggested fix is still right: skip pulled rows that have a pending `_syncQueue` entry or a newer local `updatedAt`, and run a push before the startup pull.

The finding's two-device example is the less likely path for a single-user app. The more realistic trigger is on one device: the user edits a record within about 30 s of pushing it, while a chained pull is in flight. The server-side LWW check (push/route.ts:238) rejects the stale push, so the server keeps its existing copy. The loss is of the local edit only; the server data is not corrupted. The claim that schedulePull (a microtask) runs before schedulePush(0) (a macrotask) on 'online' is correct. Startup does only a pull, with no push first.

title: Pull cursor uses client-supplied updatedAt, so offline or slow-clock writes never reach other devices
description: The server stores updatedAt as the client's wall-clock time. It only clamps values more than 60s in the future and never re-stamps with server time. Pull selects rows with updatedAt > cursor, and the cursor advances to about serverTime-30s. A row whose updatedAt falls below another device's cursor when it lands on the server is never pulled by that device. That covers records created or edited offline and pushed later, and devices whose clock is more than 30s slow. LWW also uses these client clocks, so a device with a fast clock (up to 60s) wins over genuinely later edits.

The tablet has pulled every few minutes, so its cursor is about 'now - 30s'. None of the 6 hours of records ever appear on the tablet unless it wipes _syncMeta and does a full re-pull.
suggested_fix: Add a server-assigned column (e.g. server_updated_at / a sequence) set on every write, and use it for the pull cursor. Keep client updatedAt only for LWW, or use a hybrid logical clock.
verifier_corrections:
- **Cursor position.** The cursor is not always about 'now - 30s'. It is the maximum `updatedAt` pulled so far, clamped to `serverTime - 30s` only when that row falls inside the skew window. In practice an active device pulls back its own pushed writes, which moves the cursor close to now, so the flight scenario still holds.
- **Severity.** It should be high, not critical. No data is lost or corrupted server-side; only cross-device visibility breaks.
- **Line numbers.** The `gt` filter is at `pull/route.ts` ~97-104 within the `or(...)`. The cited lines are approximately right.

The data is not lost. It is on the server and the device that wrote it, and a fresh install or a sign-out/sign-in (which clears _syncMeta) brings it back. So the right severity is high, not critical. The trigger is broader than long offline periods: any gap of more than about 30s between a local write and its push is enough, if another device pulled in between. That includes retry backoff and a closed tab that is reopened later.

Severity is overstated. Nothing is lost or corrupted on the server or on the device that wrote the rows. Other devices just never receive them, and clearing _syncMeta recovers them, so high fits better than critical. The finding also undersells how often this happens: the miss isn't limited to offline sessions or slow clocks. Any online push delayed more than about 30s after the local write can be missed by a peer that pulled in between.

title: Hard-deleted queue targets never get acked; 50 of them block all syncing
description: collectAndOrderQueuedOps takes the 50 oldest queue rows. An upsert row whose Dexie record no longer exists is skipped (`if (!liveRow) continue;`) but stays in queueRows and is never acked or dropped. If all 50 head rows are orphans, ops is empty and the cycle returns before any fetch. Every later cycle picks the same 50 rows, so nothing newer is ever pushed, and the queue depth never reaches 0. Orphans come from deletePrescription, which hard-deletes doseLogs and inventoryTransactions without enqueuing anything, and from the backup 'replace' import, which calls .clear() on every table. Writes are enqueued even in local mode, so a local-mode user has one queue row per record.
evidence: sync-engine.ts:191 `if (!liveRow) continue;` and :245 `if (ops.length === 0) { ...; return; }`. Scratch test: 50 upserts queued for missing doseLogs plus 1 real intake record; two runPushCycle calls, fetch never called, queue count stays 51.
failure_scenario: A user deletes an old prescription that had 60 dose logs queued (for example logged while offline, or in local mode before migrating). After that, no new water, dose or BP record ever syncs, and the indicator shows 'Syncing N changes…' forever.
suggested_fix: In collect, immediately ack (drop) upsert queue rows whose record is missing. Make deletePrescription soft-delete and enqueue its doseLogs and inventoryTransactions. Have backup replace/merge enqueue what it writes and tombstones what it removes.
verifier_corrections: No factual errors. One nuance: syncing stops completely only when the 50 oldest queue rows are all orphans. With fewer orphans, sync still makes progress, but queueDepth never reaches 0, so the indicator is permanently stuck on 'Syncing N changes…'. The most realistic trigger is a local-mode user who deletes a prescription and later enables cloud sync, because migration-service never clears the queue built up in local mode. The finding's scenario (a prescription deleted while already syncing) needs the dose logs to still be unpushed, for example because they were logged offline.

Minor: with fewer than 50 orphans, sync is only stuck on "Syncing…" (the pending count never reaches 0), because newer ops still fill the rest of each batch. Newer ops are fully blocked only when at least 50 orphans sit at the head of the queue. It is most reachable through backup replace (tables cleared, `_syncQueue` not), through local-mode use followed by enabling cloud sync, or through deletes made while offline. It is not reachable for an always-online signed-in user, whose queue drains within about 3 seconds.

1. The trigger is looser than the finding implies. The 50 oldest rows do not need to be orphans at the start. Each cycle acks the live rows in the head batch and leaves the orphans, so orphans pile up at the head of the queue. Once there are 50 or more orphans in total, anywhere in the queue, the queue eventually wedges.
2. There is also a milder, more common symptom the finding does not mention. Even one orphan keeps queueDepth above 0 for good, so the indicator stays on "Syncing 1 change…" even while other writes keep syncing.
3. The finding says orphans come from backup replace in general. That only happens when the imported backup lacks ids that still had pending queue rows, because replace re-adds rows with the same ids.
4. Related, not part of this finding: deletePrescription never enqueues deletes for the doseLogs and inventoryTransactions it hard-deletes, so their server copies survive.

title: Sign-out keeps local data, the queue and cursors; the next account pushes them and push's ON CONFLICT(id) re-assigns other users' rows

The server-side problem is broader than the shared-device story. Because `id` is a global primary key and `onConflictDoUpdate` has no `where` clause scoped to the owner, any whitelisted user who pushes a known foreign id can take that row over.

The claim that "two whitelisted people share a tablet" is an unrealistic premise for this single-owner app. The only realistic trigger is the owner switching to a second whitelisted account (for example the e2e test account) on the same device. The cross-account takeover can't be exploited remotely because ids are random UUIDs and the only fixed ids (preset defaults) aren't synced. The finding's "if B runs the migration" phrasing is loose: the queued ops push on their own once the engine starts. Local data isn't lost, and the damage is rows being misattributed or moved to another account in Postgres. Severity should be low, not high.

title: Migration reports success while ignoring per-row server rejections; hash verification is dead code
description: postWithRetry treats any HTTP 200 as success. /api/sync/push returns 200 with a `rejected` array for invalid rows and DB/FK failures, and the migration never reads it. The summary counts every row as 'uploaded'. verifyMigration, the only use of /api/sync/verify-hash, is never called anywhere. Even if it were, it would mismatch: client rows omit optional keys while server rows include nulls, and the server clamps updatedAt.
evidence:
migration-service.ts:73 `if (res.ok) return res;`; :128 `await postWithRetry("/api/sync/push", { ops });` (response body unused); `grep verifyMigration` shows only its definition.
---
[server-schema-parity#5] migration-service.ts:128: `await postWithRetry("/api/sync/push", { ops });` with the return value discarded.
postWithRetry: `if (res.ok) return res;`.
`grep verifyMigration` → only the definition and tests.
verify-hash/route.ts: `const { userId: _, ...rest } = row` hashes all Postgres columns, including nulls.
failure_scenario: A user with legacy rows that fail validation (e.g. NaN amounts, empty indication) migrates, sees 'Migration Complete — 4,210 records uploaded', and switches devices. Those rows are missing from the cloud, and nothing ever retries them because migration-uploaded rows have no queue entries.
suggested_fix: Parse `rejected`, surface counts and failed tables, and keep failed rows queued. Either wire in a real verification (normalise null/undefined and compare row counts) or delete verify-hash and verifyMigration.
verifier_corrections: No factual errors. I did find one more reason the hashes would not match: the client sorts rows by id with `localeCompare`, while the server uses Postgres `ORDER BY id` collation, so the two orders can differ. The 'NaN amounts' example works: NaN becomes null in JSON, and the per-op zod validation puts that row in `rejected` with code 'invalid'.
No substantive corrections. The claim that verify-hash would mismatch even if called is reasoned, not demonstrated. It does not affect the core finding, because verifyMigration is never called.

title: Rejected ops are silently dropped after 8 attempts (counter shared with network failures), and the chained pull clears the error
description: Any per-op server rejection counts toward MAX_PUSH_ATTEMPTS=8 and then drops the op for good (the local row keeps no failure marker). The attempts counter is also bumped by whole-batch network/5xx failures, so after a short outage the first transient rejection can drop an op immediately. FK ordering failures are transient: coalescing moves a parent's enqueuedAt later, pushing it out of the first 50-row batch while its children fail. Those can exhaust the budget before the parent lands. The lastError banner set by the push is cleared by the chained pull's success path about 100ms later, so the user never sees it.
evidence: sync-engine.ts:331 `if (r.code === "invalid" || nextAttempts >= MAX_PUSH_ATTEMPTS) { ... dropIds.push(q.id); }`; :397 network failures `await db._syncQueue.update(q.id, { attempts: newAttempts });`; :557 pull success `useSyncStatusStore.setState({ lastPulledAt: Date.now(), lastError: null, ... })`
failure_scenario: Offline for two days with a newly added medication, about 20 doses logged. Each dose re-enqueues the inventory item, moving it to the back. On reconnect the first 50 ops contain doses whose inventoryItem/phase is not on the server yet, so they fail the FK check and are dropped after backoff retries. The doses are never synced, and the banner flashes and disappears.
suggested_fix: Keep a separate network-failure counter. Order batches so that queued parents of included children are pulled in. Persist dropped ops to a visible 'unsynced records' list, and don't let a pull clear push errors.
verifier_corrections:
1. **"After a short outage" is too broad.** `runPushCycle` returns early when `!isOnline()`, so a true offline period (navigator offline) never bumps `attempts`. Only failed fetches or 5xx responses while the device reports online do, e.g. a server outage, captive portal or flaky connection. Rows can reach 8 attempts within a few minutes of repeated backoff (2s, 4s, … capped at 60s). After that, one rejection drops them.

2. **The FK drop comes from the re-drain loop, not slow backoff retries.** Rows that get bumped keep their old `enqueuedAt`, so they stay at the head of every 50-row batch. Whenever a cycle acks anything, it calls `schedulePush(0)` immediately, and each of those cycles bumps the stuck children again.
   - If 50 or more children are failing, the batch is the same 50 rows every time. The parent is never included, and all of them are dropped after 8 cycles.
   - If fewer are failing, each cycle adds only the few free slots of newer rows. Children are dropped when more than about 7 batches' worth of rows sit between them and the parent. That is likely after two days of offline logging, since each dose also enqueues an inventoryTransaction and an auditLog, and the parent's `enqueuedAt` keeps moving later.

3. **Minor:** the pull clears the banner on the next microtask, not about 100ms later.

- Offline periods do not bump `attempts`: `runPushCycle` bails when `!isOnline()`. Only fetch errors or 5xx while "online" share the counter.
- In the scenario given (offline two days, then reconnect), ops start at `attempts=0`. Re-drain after partial acceptance usually lets the re-enqueued parent land before the children reach 8 attempts.
- Loss needs one of two things: a large backlog (roughly more than 7 batches' worth of ops queued after the children and before the parent), or earlier transport failures that already raised `attempts`.
- The rest is accurate: the shared counter, dropping with no local marker, and the chained pull clearing `lastError`.

title: Pending queue is not flushed on app start, and queueDepth reads 0 after reload
description: startEngine only schedules a pull. Ops queued in a previous session (app killed inside the 3s debounce, or offline writes then a cold start while online) are not pushed until the next local write, visibilitychange or online event. queueDepth is ephemeral and starts at 0, so the indicator shows 'synced' while ops are pending. Meanwhile the startup pull can overwrite those pending edits (see the pull finding).
evidence: sync-engine.ts:673 `// Startup pull (D-10).\n  schedulePull();` with no schedulePush. The store default is `queueDepth: 0`.
failure_scenario: The user logs a dose and closes the PWA within 3 seconds. Next morning they open it on the phone and it shows as synced, but the dose never reaches the tablet or the server until they happen to log something else.
suggested_fix: In startEngine, call getQueueDepth() and schedulePush(0) before (or instead of) the first pull.
verifier_corrections: The finding does not apply to the native Android (Capacitor) app. There, initNetworkListener calls `Network.getStatus().then(status => callback(status.connected))` right away (network-status.ts:24-27). The engine callback runs `schedulePush(0); schedulePull();` when online (sync-engine.ts:594-598), so the queue IS flushed on a cold start there. The bug only affects the browser/PWA. The pending ops are also flushed on any later visibilitychange-to-visible, not only on the next write. The claim that the startup pull overwrites pending edits comes from a separate finding and was not checked here.

1) The finding says this happens on every platform, but it does not happen in the native Android (Capacitor) app. The Capacitor branch of initNetworkListener (network-status.ts:23-27) calls `Network.getStatus().then(status => callback(status.connected))` right after attach. That callback runs `schedulePush(0); schedulePull();` (sync-engine.ts:595-598), so the queue is flushed on start and queueDepth gets refreshed. The bug is real only for the web/PWA build.
2) The failure scenario says the dose waits "until they happen to log something else". That overstates it: any background-then-foreground (visibilitychange to visible) also triggers schedulePush(0), so the delay usually lasts until the next app switch rather than the next write. The indicator is still wrong in the meantime, and the startup pull can still clobber the pending edits first.

title: Auto-detect overrides a deliberate local-only choice and skips migration, so older local data is never uploaded
description: useSyncAutoDetect switches any 'local' device to 'cloud-sync' whenever the server holds any row for the account. It cannot tell a cold-start default from an explicit choice. The engine then starts without running migration, so only rows in _syncQueue get pushed. The queue is cleared by severSyncLink and never contains rows from before the queue existed (v16) or backup-imported rows, so that history never reaches the cloud.
evidence: use-sync-auto-detect.ts:19 `if (!authenticated || storageMode !== "local" || checked.current) return;` … `if (data?.hasSyncedData) setStorageMode("cloud-sync");`; account-service.ts:27 `await db._syncQueue.clear();`
failure_scenario: Device A switches to local and wipes the cloud. Device B, still syncing, pushes one record. On A's next launch it silently switches back to cloud-sync, and A's months of history (queue already cleared) are never uploaded.
suggested_fix: Persist whether the mode was set explicitly and only auto-restore when it wasn't. When moving to cloud-sync on a device that already has local rows, run the migration upload.
verifier_corrections: Needs a qualifier. Writes made on device A while it is in local mode still go into `_syncQueue`, because `writeWithSync` always enqueues whatever the mode is. So records created after the switch to local would be pushed once auto-detect flips the device back. What never uploads is everything that existed before the sever, plus any backup-imported rows. The finding's "older local data" wording is correct; "only rows in _syncQueue get pushed" is slightly incomplete, since that queue includes local-mode writes. Also, the flip happens on the next app launch (or remount), not the instant the other device pushes.

Small clarification: the uploaded data isn't limited to "only rows in _syncQueue" forever. New local writes made after the switch are still queued and pushed, because enqueueInsideTx runs in local mode too. What never reaches the cloud is local history from before the queue was cleared or before v16. Nothing is lost on the device itself; the gap is between devices and in the cloud copy.

title: User profile is one row per device id; a fresh device's first save wipes the other device's profile fields
description: saveUserProfile creates a new random id when no local profile exists yet. getUserProfile picks the newest active row. On a device whose pull hasn't brought the existing profile, a single toggle writes a near-empty profile (conditions: [], default consents) with a newer updatedAt, and every device switches to it.
evidence: profile-service.ts:92 `id: current.id || generateId(),` built from `current = await getUserProfile()` (the blank emptyProfile when not yet pulled); :70 `.sort((a, b) => b.updatedAt - a.updatedAt)`
failure_scenario: On a new phone the user grants AI-insights consent before the initial sync finishes. Their saved medical conditions and 'share medications' setting disappear on all devices, and AI prompts lose that context.
suggested_fix: Use a deterministic per-user profile id (e.g. a constant or the userId), and block profile saves until initialSyncComplete.
verifier_corrections: "Wipes" overstates it. The old profile row is not deleted or overwritten locally or on the server. It stays as an active row that every device ignores because the blank row has a newer updatedAt. The data is hidden, not destroyed, though users can't get it back without going to the database. The title "one row per device id" is also imprecise. A new row appears only when a device saves while it has no active profile row, i.e. before the initial pull. A device's id is not part of the key.

One small correction: the other device's profile is not wiped or deleted. Its row still exists locally and on the server with `deletedAt` null. The newer near-empty row just hides it, because `getUserProfile` shows the newest active row. Only an out-of-band fix can bring it back. A second way to hit this was left out: a device that saved a profile in local-only mode before turning on cloud sync. That path needs no race with the first sync.

title: Records-tab weight edit dialog refuses to save any weight not on a 0.1 grid (half of all weights logged at the default 0.05 increment)
description: The create form rounds weight to settings.weightIncrement, which defaults to 0.05, so values like 72.35 are normal. title: Card inline edits that clear a field only delete it locally; the server keeps the old value and the next pull restores it

Scratch test (card path): after `updateWeightRecord(id, {note: undefined})` → `note undefined has key: false` locally. sanitizeRow: `for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) { if (obj[key] === undefined || obj[key] === "") obj[key] = null; }` only covers present keys; pull: `await db.table(tn).bulkPut(rows)`.
---
[core-duplication#2] weight-card.tsx:84 `return { weight: newWeight, timestamp, note };` (note undefined when blank). push/route.ts:67 `for (const key of Object.keys(obj)) { if (obj[key] === undefined || obj[key] === "") obj[key] = null; }` ; :249 `const { id: _id, ...setValues } = writeValues;` → `.onConflictDoUpdate({ set: setValues })`. title: Records tab and HistoryDrawer carry diverging copies of all edit logic; use-record-adapters is effectively dead

title: Urination has no 'No estimate' option (defecation does); the detailed log always records an amount
description: The urination details Select is pre-filled with settings.urinationDefaultAmount and has no 'No estimate' item, even though it is labelled 'Amount (optional)'. EditUrinationDialog also has no allowNoEstimate and hard-codes its own option list instead of using URINATION_AMOUNT_OPTIONS. Defecation offers 'No estimate' on both create and edit.
evidence: urination-card: `<Label>Amount (optional)</Label><Select value={amount} ...>{AMOUNT_OPTIONS.map(...)}` with no __none__ item; defecation-card: `<SelectItem value="__none__">No estimate</SelectItem>`.

suggested_fix: Handle urination and defecation the same way: add a 'No estimate' option to urination create and edit, and use the shared constants in EditUrinationDialog.
verifier_corrections:
Minor corrections that do not change the finding:
